chapter.name: Areas Related to Circles
chapter.blurb: A circle's own area, pi r^2, is old news by Class 10 -- this chapter asks a sharper question: what is the area of just a wedge of that circle, or just the sliver cut off by a straight chord? The chapter opens by naming the two regions precisely -- a sector (bounded by two radii and an arc) and a segment (bounded by a chord and an arc) -- each with a smaller 'minor' and a larger 'major' version, then derives both the sector's area and its arc's length by the unitary method: whatever fraction the sector's angle is of a full 360-degree turn, that same fraction of the full circle's area or circumference belongs to the sector. A segment's area follows as a sector's area minus a triangle's, worked out either directly (when the central angle is 60 or 90 degrees) or, in general, by dropping a perpendicular from the centre and reaching for sine and cosine. The chapter closes with an unusually dense run of real-world sectors and segments packed into a single exercise: a grazing horse, a car's wipers, a lighthouse's warning beam, a brooch's spokes, an umbrella's ribs, and a table cover's inscribed hexagon of 'designs'.

scope_in.item: Define the sector of a circle (the region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc) and the segment of a circle (the region enclosed by a chord and the corresponding arc), and distinguish the minor and major sector, and the minor and major segment, including the convention that 'sector' and 'segment' alone mean the minor one unless stated otherwise
Identify the angle of a sector (the angle at the centre between its two radii), and use the fact that the major sector's angle is 360 degrees minus the minor sector's angle

Derive, by the unitary method from the full circle's area (pi r^2) and circumference (2 pi r) at 360 degrees, and apply the formulas for the area of a sector of angle theta -- (theta/360) x pi x r^2 -- and the length of the arc of that sector -- (theta/360) x 2 x pi x r

Use the complementary relation that the major sector's area equals pi x r^2 minus the minor sector's area, including via the alternative direct formula that uses the major sector's own angle, 360 minus theta

Find the area of a segment of a circle as (area of the sector) minus (area of the triangle formed by the chord and the two radii), and use the complementary relation that the major segment's area equals pi x r^2 minus the minor segment's area

Find the area of the triangle inside a segment for a general central angle by drawing the perpendicular from the centre to the chord, using RHS congruence to show it bisects both the chord and the central angle, and applying trigonometric ratios of the half-angle

Find the area of the triangle inside a segment directly, without trigonometry, when the central angle is 90 degrees (a right triangle formed by the two radii) or 60 degrees (an equilateral triangle, since the chord then equals the radius)
Recognise 'quadrant' (a sector of angle 90 degrees) as a term used without re-definition, assumed known from earlier classes

Solve real-world word problems that combine sector or segment areas by addition (identical non-overlapping sectors), subtraction (a change in radius at a fixed angle), or direct application at an unusual scale

Recognise that several equally spaced radii, diameters or ribs divide a circle into that many congruent sectors, and find the area of one sector, the total wire/edge length of such a figure, or the combined area of several congruent segment-shaped 'designs' formed by a regular polygon inscribed in the circle, together with a cost found from a given rate per unit area

concepts.name: Sector and segment of a circle: definitions and terms
concepts.description: The sector of a circle -- the region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc -- and the segment of a circle -- the region enclosed by a chord and the corresponding arc; the minor and major versions of each (the smaller and larger of the two regions the two radii, or the chord, divide the circle into); and the angle of a sector (the angle at the centre between its two bounding radii), including the fact that the major sector's angle is 360 degrees minus the minor sector's angle.
concepts.idea: A sector always has the centre as one of its bounding points (via the two radii), while a segment never does -- a segment is cut off entirely by a straight chord that need not pass through the centre. Unless a question says otherwise, 'sector' and 'segment' by themselves mean the minor one.
concepts.rule: Sector: the region bounded by two radii OA, OB and the arc between them; its angle is angle AOB. Segment: the region bounded by a chord AB and the arc between A and B. Both come in a minor (smaller) and major (larger) version; angle of major sector = 360 degrees - angle of minor sector.
concepts.example: In Fig. 11.1, shaded region OAPB (bounded by radii OA, OB and the minor arc APB) is the minor sector, and OAQB is the major sector. In Fig. 11.2, shaded region APB (bounded by chord AB and the minor arc) is the minor segment, and AQB is the major segment (p. 154).

concepts.name: Area of a sector and length of an arc of a circle
concepts.description: The formulas, derived by the unitary method from the full circle's own area (pi x r^2) and circumference (2 x pi x r) at 360 degrees, for the area of a sector of angle theta -- (theta/360) x pi x r^2 -- and for the length of the arc of that same sector -- (theta/360) x 2 x pi x r; and the complementary relation that the major sector's area equals pi x r^2 minus the minor sector's area.
concepts.idea: Both the sector's area and its arc's length are simply the full circle's corresponding quantity (pi x r^2, or 2 x pi x r) scaled down by the same fraction, theta/360, that the sector's angle is of a full 360-degree turn.
concepts.rule: Area of the sector of angle theta = (theta/360) x pi x r^2. Length of the arc of a sector of angle theta = (theta/360) x 2 x pi x r, where r is the radius and theta is the sector's angle in degrees. Area of major sector = pi x r^2 - area of the minor sector.
concepts.example: A sector of angle 30 degrees in a circle of radius 4 cm (pi = 3.14) has area (30/360) x 3.14 x 16 = 4.19 cm^2 (approx), and the corresponding major sector has area 3.14 x 16 - 4.19 = 46.1 cm^2 (approx) (Example 1, p. 156).

concepts.name: Area of a segment of a circle: the general method
concepts.description: The area of a segment as (area of the sector) minus (area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord); the complementary relation that the major segment's area equals pi x r^2 minus the minor segment's area; and the general method for finding that triangle's area when the central angle is not a special shortcut case -- drawing the perpendicular OM from the centre to the chord, using RHS congruence to show triangle AMO is congruent to triangle BMO (so M bisects both the chord and the angle at the centre), and then using trigonometric ratios of the half-angle to find OM and AM.
concepts.idea: Dropping a perpendicular from the centre to a chord always creates two congruent right triangles, because the two radii to the chord's ends are equal (RHS); this is what turns an awkward isosceles triangle into two easy right triangles that ordinary trigonometric ratios can handle.
concepts.rule: Area of the segment = Area of the sector - Area of the triangle formed by the chord and the two radii. Area of major segment = pi x r^2 - area of the minor segment. To find the triangle's area in general: draw OM perpendicular to chord AB; by RHS congruence, triangle AMO is congruent to triangle BMO, so angle AOM = angle BOM = half of angle AOB; then OM = r x cos(half-angle) and AM = r x sin(half-angle), giving AB = 2 x AM and triangle area = (1/2) x AB x OM.
concepts.example: For a chord subtending 120 degrees in a circle of radius 21 cm (pi = 22/7): sector area = 462 cm^2; OM = 21 x cos 60 degrees = 10.5 cm, AM = 21 x sin 60 degrees = 10.5 x square root of 3 cm, so the triangle's area is 441 x square root of 3 / 4 cm^2, and the segment's area is (462 - 441 x square root of 3 / 4) cm^2, approximately 271.05 cm^2 (Example 2, p. 157-158).

concepts.name: Area of a segment at standard angles (60, 90 degrees): shortcut triangle formulas
concepts.description: Two special cases where the triangle inside a segment can be found directly, without drawing a perpendicular or using trigonometry: when the chord subtends 90 degrees at the centre, the two radii themselves are perpendicular, giving a simple right triangle of area (1/2) x r^2; and when the chord subtends 60 degrees, the isosceles triangle of two radii and equal base angles becomes fully equilateral (all sides equal r), giving area (square root of 3 / 4) x r^2.
concepts.idea: These are not new formulas so much as the same 'sector minus triangle' idea applied at a shortcut angle, where the triangle's shape is already familiar (right-angled, or equilateral) so its area can be written down directly.
concepts.rule: For a chord subtending 90 degrees at the centre: triangle area = (1/2) x r x r = r^2/2 (the two radii are the base and height). For a chord subtending 60 degrees at the centre: the triangle is equilateral with side r, so triangle area = (square root of 3 / 4) x r^2. In both cases, segment area = sector area - triangle area, exactly as in the general method.
concepts.example: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtending a right angle at the centre (pi = 3.14) has minor segment area = 78.5 - 50 = 28.5 cm^2 (Exercise 11.1, Q4). A chord of a circle of radius 15 cm subtending 60 degrees (pi = 3.14, square root of 3 = 1.73) has minor segment area = 117.75 - 97.3125 = 20.4375 cm^2 (Exercise 11.1, Q6).

concepts.name: Combining and comparing sector areas in real-world problems
concepts.description: Using addition, subtraction, or direct application of the sector-area formula to solve real-world problems: adding the areas of two or more identical, non-overlapping sector-shaped regions (such as two car wipers); finding the increase or decrease in a sector-shaped area when only the radius changes and the angle stays fixed (such as an animal's grazing area when its rope is lengthened); and applying the same formula directly at an unusual real-world scale (such as a lighthouse's beam over the sea, measured in kilometres).
concepts.idea: The sector-area formula itself never changes; what changes in these problems is recognising, from the real-world description, what plays the role of the radius and the angle, and whether the situation calls for adding two areas, subtracting one from another, or just reading off a single area.
concepts.rule: Total area of several identical, non-overlapping sectors = (one sector's area) x (the number of sectors). Increase in area from a radius change (angle fixed) = (area with the new radius) - (area with the old radius). Otherwise, apply (theta/360) x pi x r^2 directly with the radius and angle the real-world situation describes.
concepts.example: A horse tied by a 5 m rope at a corner of a square field (a 90-degree sector, since a square's corner is a right angle) can graze 19.625 m^2 (pi = 3.14); with a 10 m rope instead, it can graze 78.5 m^2, an increase of 58.875 m^2 (Exercise 11.1, Q8).

concepts.description: Recognising that several equally spaced radii, diameters or ribs divide a circle into that many congruent sectors, each of angle 360/n degrees and area (whole circle's area)/n; finding the total wire or edge length of such a figure, made of the circle's own circumference plus any internal straight radii or diameters; and finding the combined area of several congruent segment-shaped 'design' regions formed between a circle and a regular polygon inscribed in it, as (circle's area) minus (polygon's area), then applying a cost rate to that area.
concepts.idea: Equally spaced radii, diameters or ribs cut sectors, which divide the circle's area by simple counting (area of one = total/n); but points on the rim joined to each other by straight chords, not to the centre, cut segments instead, whose combined area is the circle's area minus the polygon those chords trace out -- these two situations look similar but use different arithmetic.
concepts.rule: n equally spaced radii divide a circle into n congruent sectors, each of angle 360/n degrees and area (pi x r^2)/n. Total wire for a circle plus m diameters = circumference (pi x d) + m x (length of one diameter). Combined area of k congruent segment 'designs' cut off by a regular k-sided polygon inscribed in a circle = (circle's area) - (polygon's area); cost = that area x the given rate per unit area.
concepts.example: A brooch of diameter 35 mm with 5 diameters (10 sectors of 36 degrees each) needs 285 mm of wire and has 96.25 mm^2 per sector (Exercise 11.1, Q9). A round table cover of radius 28 cm with six equal designs (an inscribed regular hexagon; pi = 22/7, square root of 3 = 1.7) has combined design area 464.8 cm^2, costing Rs 162.68 at Rs 0.35 per cm^2 (Exercise 11.1, Q13).
